title: Einhänder
subtitle: One arm for the next weapon
summary: Einhänder is Square's PlayStation scrolling shooter, released in Japan on 20 November 1997. A pilot from the Moon enters enemy territory on Earth during a future war, gathering information and weapons. The spacecraft's single manipulator arm supplies the game's name and central action: enemy gunpods can be taken and attached to the fighter. Three-dimensional scenery changes the camera's view, while movement remains on a two-dimensional plane. The result gives a familiar side-scrolling advance a changing sense of scale as buildings, machinery and hostile craft pass around the player.
body: Einhänder is Square's PlayStation scrolling shooter, released in Japan on 20 November 1997. A pilot from the Moon enters enemy territory on Earth during a future war, gathering information and weapons. The spacecraft's single manipulator arm supplies the game's name and central action: enemy gunpods can be taken and attached to the fighter. Three-dimensional scenery changes the camera's view, while movement remains on a two-dimensional plane. The result gives a familiar side-scrolling advance a changing sense of scale as buildings, machinery and hostile craft pass around the player.

A standard machine gun remains available, but captured gunpods provide weapons with different reach, ammunition and power. A cannon, guided missiles or a large energy blade changes the useful distance from a target. The arm can hold a pod above or below the craft, altering its firing angle or direction. Ammunition runs out, so a powerful attachment is also a temporary opportunity. Choosing when to use it and where to carry it ties the next attack to what enemies have already left behind, rather than to a fixed selection made before the stage.

Destroying enemy cores builds a hit counter and increases the points awarded for further cores. Hesitation lets that counter fall; reaching a high multiplier creates a short period of larger bonuses. Bosses often have separate parts around a main core, giving the player several things to read and dismantle during one confrontation. Kenichiro Fukui's techno- and trance-oriented score supports the mechanical setting. Critics praised the graphics and shooting, while noting the short duration and lack of two-player play. The North American release followed in May 1998, with the original game later returning on Japan's PlayStation Network.
